name: INA4180A2IPWR
title: 26 V common-mode, fixed-gain voltage-output current-sense amplifiers, one, two and four channels
summary: INA180, INA2180 and INA4180 amplify the voltage across a current shunt and give a ground-referred output voltage. Inputs work from -0.2 V to +26 V common mode independent of the 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply, so the shunt can be on the high or low side. Gain is fixed at 20, 50, 100 or 200 V/V (A1 to A4) by matched internal resistors, with ±1% maximum gain error and up to 350 kHz bandwidth. INA2180A1IDGKR is the dual-channel, gain-20 part in VSSOP-8 on a 2500-piece reel.
key_figures: ±150 µV max at VIN+ = 0 V; ±500 µV max at 12 V

circuits.title: Basic connections, high-side sensing into an ADC
circuits.description: A shunt RSENSE sits between the bus (-0.2 V to +26 V) and the load, whose return is ground. IN+ takes the bus end of the shunt and IN- the load end, so the shunt voltage times the gain appears at OUT, which feeds the ADC input of a microcontroller. The amplifier runs from its own 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply with C1 from VS to ground. The ADC reference or microcontroller ground should join as near the GND pin as possible, and an RC filter between OUT and the ADC is advised.
notes: Pin names are those of the INA180; the same connections apply to each channel of the INA2180 and INA4180.

circuits.title: Low-side sensing
circuits.description: The shunt is the last element in the load's return path: the load runs from its supply into RSENSE, and RSENSE goes to ground. IN+ takes the load end of the shunt and IN- the grounded end, so the common-mode voltage sits near 0 V. VOUT is the shunt voltage times the gain; C1 bypasses VS. The worked example in the equations section sizes RSENSE and the gain for this circuit.

parts.note: value chosen in the worked example

notes: The worked example uses the INA180A4 (gain 200) at VS = 5 V.

circuits.title: Shutdown by switching the supply
circuits.description: The part has no shutdown pin, so a P-channel MOSFET Q1 switches its supply. Q1's source is on the 2.7 V to 5.5 V rail and its drain feeds VS, with C1 from VS to ground. A 10 kΩ resistor runs from Q1's gate to its source, and the Shutdown line drives the gate. The sensing side is a high-side shunt between the bus and the load.

circuits.title: Differential filter at the input pins
circuits.description: A high-side shunt between the bus and the load drives the inputs through a series resistor RF in each line, under 10 Ω, with CF across the two filtered nodes at IN- and IN+. The corner is f-3dB = 1 / (2π (RF + RF) CF). Each RF adds gain error through the internal input resistance; the gain error factor equations give its size. VOUT is OUT; C1 bypasses VS.

circuits.title: Transient protection with two Zener diodes
circuits.description: For common-mode transients above 26 V, each input is fed through RPROTECT (10 Ω or less) and clamped to ground by its own Zener diode, cathode at the input, anode at ground. The resistors give the Zeners a working impedance. The shunt is on the high side between the bus and the load; C1 bypasses VS and OUT is the output.

circuits.title: Transient protection with one transzorb and input clamps
circuits.description: Where small Zeners cannot absorb the transient energy, one bidirectional transzorb clamps the IN- node to ground and two clamp diodes in opposite directions sit between IN- and IN+. Each input line has a series resistor under 10 Ω. The shunt is on the high side between the bus and the load; C1 bypasses VS and OUT is the output.

operation.text: INA180 (one channel, SOT-23-5), INA2180 (two, VSSOP-8 or WSON-8) and INA4180 (four, TSSOP-14) are fixed-gain current-sense amplifiers. Each comes in gains of 20 (A1), 50 (A2), 100 (A3) and 200 (A4) V/V set by an on-chip matched resistor network. The INA180 has two pinouts, A and B. All run from 2.7 V to 5.5 V and are specified from -40°C to +125°C. Automotive versions are INA180-Q1, INA2180-Q1 and INA4180-Q1.

The inputs work from -0.2 V to +26 V common mode whatever the supply, as long as VS is within 2.7 V to 5.5 V, so the same part serves high-side and low-side shunts. High side, the common-mode voltage follows the bus; low side it stays near ground, away from bus spikes. The inputs tolerate up to 26 V differential and common mode whether or not VS is powered.
Small-signal bandwidth reaches 350 kHz (A1) and the output slews at 2 V/µs, which suits low-side motor control and fast fault detection with an external comparator and reference.
At low common-mode voltage the offset is within ±150 µV, which keeps small currents accurate and allows a smaller shunt with less loss. At large signals the gain error, within 1%, dominates.

The output reaches within 30 mV of VS and 5 mV of ground, measured with the input overdriven. In closed loop, the low limit is the larger of the specified swing to GND and offset times gain when the offset is positive: an INA180A4 with +40 µV offset bottoms at 8 mV; with -40 µV it reaches the specified swing. Offset grows with common-mode voltage through CMRR, raising the zero-current output at high common mode.

The part measures correctly when VS is 2.7 V to 5.5 V, VCM is -0.2 V to +26 V, the largest differential input times gain stays below VS less the swing to VS, and the smallest stays above the swing to GND. The output is then the IN+ to IN- difference times the gain.

If differential input times gain exceeds the swing range, the output goes as near the positive rail as it can and stops tracking. If this happens in normal use, a smaller shunt or lower gain is called for. After a fault-driven overload clears, the output returns to its correct value in about 20 µs. Within the absolute maximum ratings the overload causes no damage and the output keeps its polarity, with no phase reversal.

There is no shutdown pin; the supply can be switched by a logic gate or transistor since the quiescent current is small. Unpowered, each input sees more than 500 kΩ (the feedback and input resistors) to OUT and to GND, and the disabled output stage is a good path to ground, so input current is the shunt common-mode voltage over about 500 kΩ. When powered and the common-mode voltage is above VS, a further matched current of about 55 µA typical flows into each input; below VS it is negligible.

A larger shunt raises the signal and cuts the share of offset error, but the inputs draw about 80 µA each at 12 V common mode, so shunts above a few ohms add offset error and degrade CMRR. The shunt is also limited by its dissipation budget, and with the gain by the positive and negative swing limits.

With a high-impedance load on OUT, an RC from OUT to GND is the best filter: it attenuates disturbances from common mode, the differential signal and the supply together. A filter at the input pins is possible when only the differential signal needs filtering, but series resistors should be 10 Ω or less: the internal bias network makes the two input currents unequal under a differential signal, and the unequal drops across the resistors show up as gain error.

VS = 5 V, VCM = 0 V, 40 A, under 900 mW in the shunt, under 1.5% error, over 80 kHz. The dissipation limit gives 0.563 mΩ; 0.5 mΩ is chosen. The swing limit allows a gain up to 248.5, so the INA180A4 (200) is used. Offset error with 150 µV is 0.75%; with 1% gain error the root-sum-square total is 1.25%. The A4 bandwidth of 105 kHz meets the 80 kHz need.
The output sits at its low limit near ground with zero input; it rises for positive differential input and cannot go below ground for negative input.

The output range is bounded by VS while the inputs may sit well above it, for example VS = 5 V with a 26 V bus. VS needs at least 0.1 µF of bypass capacitance; noisy or high-impedance supplies may need more.

Only Zener diodes or Zener-type absorbers are fast enough; other absorbers respond too late. A series resistor in each input, usually about 10 Ω, gives the Zener a working impedance; larger values add gain error. Since only short transients are clamped, low-power Zeners in SOT-523 or SOD-523 are often enough. For more energy, one transzorb with back-to-back diodes between the inputs is the compact choice. Either way the part and its protection take less board area than an SO-8.

Connect the inputs to the shunt with a Kelvin (4-wire) connection so only the shunt resistance lies between them; extra copper in the high-current path causes large errors with low-value shunts. Keep the two sense traces matched in length. Mount the 0.1 µF bypass capacitor right at the VS and GND pins, adding more for noisy or high-impedance supplies. The ADC reference or microcontroller ground should join near the GND pin. On the WSON-8 the exposed pad may be left floating or tied to GND.
